segs.e: Linked Discourses 15.1
Chapter One
Grass and Sticks
So I have heard.

segs.p: ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṁ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,
“Mendicants!”
“Venerable sir,” they replied.
The Buddha said this:
“Mendicants, this transmigration has no known beginning.

segs.p: Pubbā koṭi na paññāyati avijjānīvaraṇānaṁ sattānaṁ taṇhāsaṁyojanānaṁ sandhāvataṁ saṁsarataṁ.
segs.e: No first point is found of sentient beings roaming and transmigrating, shrouded by ignorance and fettered by craving.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso yaṁ imasmiṁ jambudīpe tiṇakaṭṭhasākhāpalāsaṁ taṁ chetvā ekajjhaṁ saṁharitvā caturaṅgulaṁ caturaṅgulaṁ ghaṭikaṁ katvā nikkhipeyya:
segs.e: Suppose a person was to strip all the grass, sticks, branches, and leaves in the Black Plum Tree Land, gather them together into one pile, and chop them each into four inch pieces. They’d lay them down, saying:

segs.p: ‘ayaṁ me mātā, tassā me mātu ayaṁ mātā’ti, apariyādinnāva, bhikkhave, tassa purisassa mātumātaro assu, atha imasmiṁ jambudīpe tiṇakaṭṭhasākhāpalāsaṁ parikkhayaṁ pariyādānaṁ gaccheyya.
segs.e: ‘This is my mother, this is my grandmother.’ The grass, sticks, branches, and leaves of the Black Plum Tree Land would run out before that person’s mothers and grandmothers.
Why is that?
This transmigration has no known beginning.

segs.p: Pubbā koṭi na paññāyati avijjānīvaraṇānaṁ sattānaṁ taṇhāsaṁyojanānaṁ sandhāvataṁ saṁsarataṁ.
segs.e: No first point is found of sentient beings roaming and transmigrating, shrouded by ignorance and fettered by craving.

segs.p: Evaṁ dīgharattaṁ vo, bhikkhave, dukkhaṁ paccanubhūtaṁ tibbaṁ paccanubhūtaṁ byasanaṁ paccanubhūtaṁ, kaṭasī vaḍḍhitā.
segs.e: For such a long time you have undergone suffering, agony, and disaster, swelling the cemeteries.

segs.p: Yāvañcidaṁ, bhikkhave, alameva sabbasaṅkhāresu nibbindituṁ alaṁ virajjituṁ alaṁ vimuccitun”ti.
segs.e: This is quite enough for you to become disillusioned, dispassionate, and freed regarding all conditions.”
Linked Discourses 15.2
Chapter One
The Earth
At Sāvatthī.
“Mendicants, this transmigration has no known beginning.

segs.p: Pubbā koṭi na paññāyati avijjānīvaraṇānaṁ sattānaṁ taṇhāsaṁyojanānaṁ sandhāvataṁ saṁsarataṁ.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, puriso imaṁ mahāpathaviṁ kolaṭṭhimattaṁ kolaṭṭhimattaṁ mattikāguḷikaṁ karitvā nikkhipeyya:
segs.e: Suppose a person was to make the whole earth into clay balls the size of jujube seeds. They’d lay them down, saying:

segs.p: ‘ayaṁ me pitā, tassa me pitu ayaṁ pitā’ti, apariyādinnāva bhikkhave, tassa purisassa pitupitaro assu, athāyaṁ mahāpathavī parikkhayaṁ pariyādānaṁ gaccheyya.
segs.e: ‘This is my father, this is my grandfather.’ The whole earth would run out before that person’s fathers and grandfathers.
Why is that?
This transmigration has no known beginning.

segs.p: Yāvañcidaṁ, bhikkhave, alameva sabbasaṅkhāresu nibbindituṁ, alaṁ virajjituṁ, alaṁ vimuccitun”ti.

Linked Discourses 15.3
Chapter One
Tears
At Sāvatthī.
“Mendicants, this transmigration has no known beginning.

segs.p: Pubbā koṭi na paññāyati avijjānīvaraṇānaṁ sattānaṁ taṇhāsaṁyojanānaṁ sandhāvataṁ saṁsarataṁ.
segs.e: No first point is found of sentient beings roaming and transmigrating, shrouded by ignorance and fettered by craving.

segs.p: Taṁ kiṁ maññatha, bhikkhave, katamaṁ nu kho bahutaraṁ, yaṁ vā vo iminā dīghena addhunā sandhāvataṁ saṁsarataṁ amanāpasampayogā manāpavippayogā kandantānaṁ rodantānaṁ assu passannaṁ paggharitaṁ, yaṁ vā catūsu mahāsamuddesu udakan”ti?
segs.e: What do you think? Which is more: the flow of tears you’ve shed while roaming and transmigrating for such a very long time—weeping and wailing from being coupled with the unloved and separated from the loved—or the water in the four oceans?”

segs.p: “Yathā kho mayaṁ, bhante, bhagavatā dhammaṁ desitaṁ ājānāma, etadeva, bhante, bahutaraṁ yaṁ no iminā dīghena addhunā sandhāvataṁ saṁsarataṁ amanāpasampayogā manāpavippayogā kandantānaṁ rodantānaṁ assu passannaṁ paggharitaṁ, na tveva catūsu mahāsamuddesu udakan”ti.
segs.e: “As we understand the Buddha’s teaching, the flow of tears we’ve shed while roaming and transmigrating is more than the water in the four oceans.”

segs.p: “Sādhu sādhu, bhikkhave, sādhu kho me tumhe, bhikkhave, evaṁ dhammaṁ desitaṁ ājānātha.
segs.e: “Good, good, mendicants! It’s good that you understand my teaching like this.

segs.p: Etadeva, bhikkhave, bahutaraṁ yaṁ vo iminā dīghena addhunā sandhāvataṁ saṁsarataṁ amanāpasampayogā manāpavippayogā kandantānaṁ rodantānaṁ assu passannaṁ paggharitaṁ, na tveva catūsu mahāsamuddesu udakaṁ.
segs.e: The flow of tears you’ve shed while roaming and transmigrating is indeed more than the water in the four oceans.
For a long time you’ve undergone the death of a mother …

segs.p: tesaṁ vo mātumaraṇaṁ paccanubhontānaṁ amanāpasampayogā manāpavippayogā kandantānaṁ rodantānaṁ assu passannaṁ paggharitaṁ, na tveva catūsu mahāsamuddesu udakaṁ.

segs.e: father …
brother …
sister …
son …
daughter …
loss of relatives …
loss of wealth …

segs.p: Dīgharattaṁ vo, bhikkhave, rogabyasanaṁ paccanubhūtaṁ, tesaṁ vo rogabyasanaṁ paccanubhontānaṁ amanāpasampayogā manāpavippayogā kandantānaṁ rodantānaṁ assu passannaṁ paggharitaṁ, na tveva catūsu mahāsamuddesu udakaṁ.
segs.e: or loss through illness. From being coupled with the unloved and separated from the loved, the flow of tears you’ve shed while roaming and transmigrating is indeed more than the water in the four oceans.
Why is that?
This transmigration has no known beginning. …

segs.p: yāvañcidaṁ, bhikkhave, alameva sabbasaṅkhāresu nibbindituṁ, alaṁ virajjituṁ, alaṁ vimuccitun”ti.
segs.e: This is quite enough for you to become disillusioned, dispassionate, and freed regarding all conditions.”

At Sāvatthī.
“Mendicants, this transmigration has no known beginning.

Linked Discourses 15.5
Chapter One
A Mountain
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: Atha kho aññataro bhikkhu yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho so bhikkhu bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then a mendicant went up to the Buddha, bowed, sat down to one side, and asked him,
“Sir, how long is an eon?”
“Mendicant, an eon is long.

segs.p: So na sukaro saṅkhātuṁ ettakāni vassāni iti vā, ettakāni vassasatāni iti vā, ettakāni vassasahassāni iti vā, ettakāni vassasatasahassāni iti vā”ti.
segs.e: It’s not easy to calculate how many years, how many hundreds or thousands or hundreds of thousands of years it lasts.”
“But sir, is it possible to give a simile?”
“It’s possible,” said the Buddha.

segs.p: “Seyyathāpi, bhikkhu, mahāselo pabbato yojanaṁ āyāmena yojanaṁ vitthārena yojanaṁ ubbedhena acchinno asusiro ekagghano.
segs.e: “Suppose there was a big rocky mountain, a league long, a league wide, and a league high, with no cracks or holes, one solid mass.

segs.p: Tamenaṁ puriso vassasatassa vassasatassa accayena kāsikena vatthena sakiṁ sakiṁ parimajjeyya.
segs.e: And as each century passed someone would stroke it once with a fine cloth from Kāsi.

segs.p: Khippataraṁ kho so, bhikkhu, mahāselo pabbato iminā upakkamena parikkhayaṁ pariyādānaṁ gaccheyya, na tveva kappo.
segs.e: By this means the big rocky mountain would be worn away before the eon comes to an end.
That’s how long an eon is.

segs.p: Evaṁ dīghānaṁ kho, bhikkhu, kappānaṁ neko kappo saṁsito, nekaṁ kappasataṁ saṁsitaṁ, nekaṁ kappasahassaṁ saṁsitaṁ, nekaṁ kappasatasahassaṁ saṁsitaṁ.
segs.e: And we’ve transmigrated through many such eons, many hundreds, many thousands, many hundreds of thousands.
Why is that?
This transmigration has no known beginning. …

segs.p: yāvañcidaṁ, bhikkhu, alameva sabbasaṅkhāresu nibbindituṁ, alaṁ virajjituṁ, alaṁ vimuccitun”ti.
segs.e: This is quite enough for you to become disillusioned, dispassionate, and freed regarding all conditions.”
Linked Discourses 15.6
Chapter One
A Mustard Seed
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: Atha kho aññataro bhikkhu yena bhagavā …pe… ekamantaṁ nisinno kho so bhikkhu bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: Then a mendicant went up to the Buddha … and asked him,
“Sir, how long is an eon?”
“Mendicant, an eon is long.

segs.p: So na sukaro saṅkhātuṁ ettakāni vassāni iti vā …pe… ettakāni vassasatasahassāni iti vā”ti.
segs.e: It’s not easy to calculate how many years, how many hundreds or thousands or hundreds of thousands of years it lasts.”
“But sir, is it possible to give a simile?”
“It’s possible,” said the Buddha.

segs.p: “Seyyathāpi, bhikkhu, āyasaṁ nagaraṁ yojanaṁ āyāmena yojanaṁ vitthārena yojanaṁ ubbedhena, puṇṇaṁ sāsapānaṁ guḷikābaddhaṁ.
segs.e: “Suppose there was an iron citadel, a league long, a league wide, and a league high, full of mustard seeds pressed into balls.

segs.p: Tato puriso vassasatassa vassasatassa accayena ekamekaṁ sāsapaṁ uddhareyya.
segs.e: And as each century passed someone would remove a single mustard seed.

segs.p: Khippataraṁ kho so, bhikkhu, mahāsāsaparāsi iminā upakkamena parikkhayaṁ pariyādānaṁ gaccheyya, na tveva kappo.
segs.e: By this means the big heap of mustard seeds would be used up before the eon comes to an end.
That’s how long an eon is.

segs.p: Evaṁ dīghānaṁ kho, bhikkhu, kappānaṁ neko kappo saṁsito, nekaṁ kappasataṁ saṁsitaṁ, nekaṁ kappasahassaṁ saṁsitaṁ, nekaṁ kappasatasahassaṁ saṁsitaṁ.
segs.e: And we’ve transmigrated through many such eons, many hundreds, many thousands, many hundreds of thousands.
Why is that?
This transmigration has no known beginning. …
This is quite enough for you to become disillusioned, dispassionate, and freed regarding all conditions.”
Linked Discourses 15.7
Chapter One
Disciples
At Sāvatthī.

segs.p: Atha kho sambahulā bhikkhū yena bhagavā …pe… ekamantaṁ nisinnā kho te bhikkhū bhagavantaṁ etadavocuṁ:
segs.e: Then several mendicants went up to the Buddha … and asked him,

segs.p: “kīvabahukā nu kho, bhante, kappā abbhatītā atikkantā”ti?
segs.e: “Sir, how many eons have passed?”
“Mendicants, many eons have passed.
It’s not easy to calculate

segs.p: ‘ettakā kappā iti vā, ettakāni kappasatāni iti vā, ettakāni kappasahassāni iti vā, ettakāni kappasatasahassāni iti vā’”ti.
segs.e: how many eons have passed, how many hundreds or thousands or hundreds of thousands of eons.”
“But sir, is it possible to give a simile?”
“It’s possible,” said the Buddha.
“Suppose there were four disciples with a lifespan of a hundred years.

segs.p: Te divase divase kappasatasahassaṁ kappasatasahassaṁ anussareyyuṁ.
segs.e: And each day they would each recollect a hundred thousand eons.

segs.p: Ananussaritāva, bhikkhave, tehi kappā assu, atha kho te cattāro sāvakā vassasatāyukā vassasatajīvino vassasatassa accayena kālaṁ kareyyuṁ.
segs.e: Those four disciples would pass away after a hundred years and there would still be eons that they haven’t recollected.

segs.p: Evaṁ bahukā kho, bhikkhave, kappā abbhatītā atikkantā.
segs.e: That’s how many eons have passed.
It’s not easy to calculate

segs.p: ‘ettakā kappā iti vā, ettakāni kappasatāni iti vā, ettakāni kappasahassāni iti vā, ettakāni kappasatasahassāni iti vā’ti.
segs.e: how many eons have passed, how many hundreds or thousands or hundreds of thousands of eons.
Why is that?
This transmigration has no known beginning. …
This is quite enough for you to become disillusioned, dispassionate, and freed regarding all conditions.”
Linked Discourses 15.8
Chapter One
The Ganges
Near Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove.

segs.p: Atha kho aññataro brāhmaṇo yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkami; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavatā saddhiṁ sammodi.
segs.e: Then a certain brahmin went up to the Buddha, and exchanged greetings with him.

segs.p: Sammodanīyaṁ kathaṁ sāraṇīyaṁ vītisāretvā ekamantaṁ nisīdi. Ekamantaṁ nisinno kho so brāhmaṇo bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: When the greetings and polite conversation were over, he sat down to one side and asked the Buddha,

segs.p: “kīvabahukā nu kho, bho gotama, kappā abbhatītā atikkantā”ti?
segs.e: “Worthy Gotama, how many eons have passed?”
“Brahmin, many eons have passed.
It’s not easy to calculate

segs.p: ‘ettakā kappā iti vā, ettakāni kappasatāni iti vā, ettakāni kappasahassāni iti vā, ettakāni kappasatasahassāni iti vā’”ti.
segs.e: how many eons have passed, how many hundreds or thousands or hundreds of thousands of eons.”
“But worthy Gotama, can you give a simile?”
“I can,” said the Buddha.

segs.p: “Seyyathāpi, brāhmaṇa, yato cāyaṁ gaṅgā nadī pabhavati yattha ca mahāsamuddaṁ appeti, yā etasmiṁ antare vālikā sā na sukarā saṅkhātuṁ:
segs.e: “Consider the Ganges River from where it originates to where it meets the ocean. Between these places it’s not easy to calculate

segs.p: ‘ettakā vālikā iti vā, ettakāni vālikasatāni iti vā, ettakāni vālikasahassāni iti vā, ettakāni vālikasatasahassāni iti vā’ti.
segs.e: how many grains of sand there are, how many hundreds or thousands or hundreds of thousands of grains of sand.

segs.p: Tato bahutarā kho, brāhmaṇa, kappā abbhatītā atikkantā.
segs.e: The eons that have passed are more than this.
It’s not easy to calculate

segs.p: ‘ettakā kappā iti vā, ettakāni kappasatāni iti vā, ettakāni kappasahassāni iti vā, ettakāni kappasatasahassāni iti vā’ti.
segs.e: how many eons have passed, how many hundreds or thousands or hundreds of thousands of eons.
Why is that?
This transmigration has no known beginning.

segs.p: Pubbā koṭi na paññāyati avijjānīvaraṇānaṁ sattānaṁ taṇhāsaṁyojanānaṁ sandhāvataṁ saṁsarataṁ.
segs.e: No first point is found of sentient beings roaming and transmigrating, shrouded by ignorance and fettered by craving.

segs.p: Evaṁ dīgharattaṁ kho, brāhmaṇa, dukkhaṁ paccanubhūtaṁ tibbaṁ paccanubhūtaṁ byasanaṁ paccanubhūtaṁ, kaṭasī vaḍḍhitā.
segs.e: For such a long time you have undergone suffering, agony, and disaster, swelling the cemeteries.

segs.p: Yāvañcidaṁ, brāhmaṇa, alameva sabbasaṅkhāresu nibbindituṁ, alaṁ virajjituṁ, alaṁ vimuccitun”ti.
segs.e: This is quite enough for you to become disillusioned, dispassionate, and freed regarding all conditions.”

segs.p: Evaṁ vutte, so brāhmaṇo bhagavantaṁ etadavoca:
segs.e: When he said this, the brahmin said to the Buddha,
“Excellent, worthy Gotama! Excellent! …

segs.p: upāsakaṁ maṁ bhavaṁ gotamo dhāretu ajjatagge pāṇupetaṁ saraṇaṁ gatan”ti.
segs.e: From this day forth, may the worthy Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge for life.”
Linked Discourses 15.9
Chapter One
A Stick
At Sāvatthī.
“Mendicants, this transmigration has no known beginning.

segs.p: Pubbā koṭi na paññāyati avijjānīvaraṇānaṁ sattānaṁ taṇhāsaṁyojanānaṁ sandhāvataṁ saṁsarataṁ.
segs.e: No first point is found of sentient beings roaming and transmigrating, shrouded by ignorance and fettered by craving.

segs.p: Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, daṇḍo uparivehāsaṁ khitto sakimpi mūlena nipatati, sakimpi majjhena nipatati, sakimpi antena nipatati;
segs.e: Suppose a stick was tossed up in the air. Sometimes it’d fall on its bottom, sometimes the middle, and sometimes the end.

segs.p: evameva kho, bhikkhave, avijjānīvaraṇā sattā taṇhāsaṁyojanā sandhāvantā saṁsarantā sakimpi asmā lokā paraṁ lokaṁ gacchanti, sakimpi parasmā lokā imaṁ lokaṁ āgacchanti.
segs.e: It’s the same for sentient beings roaming and transmigrating, shrouded by ignorance and fettered by craving. Sometimes they go from this world to the other world, and sometimes they come from the other world to this world.
Why is that?
This transmigration has no known beginning. …
This is quite enough for you to become disillusioned, dispassionate, and freed regarding all conditions.”
Linked Discourses 15.10
Chapter One
A Single Individual

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā rājagahe viharati gijjhakūṭe pabbate.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain.
There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,
“Mendicants!”
“Venerable sir,” they replied.
The Buddha said this:
“Mendicants, this transmigration has no known beginning. …

segs.p: ekapuggalassa, bhikkhave, kappaṁ sandhāvato saṁsarato siyā evaṁ mahā aṭṭhikaṅkalo aṭṭhipuñjo aṭṭhirāsi yathāyaṁ vepullo pabbato, sace saṁhārako assa, sambhatañca na vinasseyya.
segs.e: One individual roaming and transmigrating for an eon would amass a heap of bones the size of this Mount Vepulla, if they were gathered together and not lost.
Why is that?
This transmigration has no known beginning. …
This is quite enough for you to become disillusioned, dispassionate, and freed regarding all conditions.”
That is what the Buddha said.

segs.p: Idaṁ vatvāna sugato athāparaṁ etadavoca satthā:
segs.e: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:
“If the bones of a single individual
for a single eon were gathered up,
they’d make a pile the size of a mountain:
so said the great seer.
And this is declared to be
as big as Mount Vepulla,
higher than the Vulture’s Peak
in the Mountainfold of the Magadhans.
But then, with right understanding,
one sees the noble truths—
suffering, suffering’s origin,
suffering’s transcendence,
and the noble eightfold path
that leads to the stilling of suffering.
After roaming on seven times at most,
that individual
makes an end of suffering,
with the ending of all fetters.”
Linked Discourses 15.11
Chapter Two
In a Sorry State
At one time the Buddha was staying near Sāvatthī.
“Mendicants, this transmigration has no known beginning.

segs.p: Pubbā koṭi na paññāyati avijjānīvaraṇānaṁ sattānaṁ taṇhāsaṁyojanānaṁ sandhāvataṁ saṁsarataṁ.
segs.e: No first point is found of sentient beings roaming and transmigrating, shrouded by ignorance and fettered by craving.

segs.p: Yaṁ, bhikkhave, passeyyātha duggataṁ durūpetaṁ niṭṭhamettha gantabbaṁ:
segs.e: When you see someone in a sorry state, in distress, you should conclude:
‘In all this long time, we too have undergone the same thing.’
Why is that? This transmigration has no known beginning. …

segs.p: yāvañcidaṁ, bhikkhave, alameva sabbasaṅkhāresu nibbindituṁ alaṁ virajjituṁ alaṁ vimuccitun”ti.
segs.e: This is quite enough for you to become disillusioned, dispassionate, and freed regarding all conditions.”
Linked Discourses 15.12
Chapter Two
In a Good Way
At Sāvatthī.
“Mendicants, this transmigration has no known beginning. …

segs.p: yaṁ, bhikkhave, passeyyātha sukhitaṁ susajjitaṁ, niṭṭhamettha gantabbaṁ:
segs.e: When you see someone in a good way, in a happy state, you should conclude:
‘In all this long time, we too have undergone the same thing.’
Why is that?
This transmigration has no known beginning. …
This is quite enough for you to become disillusioned, dispassionate, and freed regarding all conditions.”
Linked Discourses 15.13
Chapter Two
Thirty Mendicants
Near Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove.

segs.p: Atha kho tiṁsamattā pāveyyakā bhikkhū sabbe āraññikā sabbe piṇḍapātikā sabbe paṁsukūlikā sabbe tecīvarikā sabbe sasaṁyojanā yena bhagavā tenupasaṅkamiṁsu; upasaṅkamitvā bhagavantaṁ abhivādetvā ekamantaṁ nisīdiṁsu.
segs.e: Then thirty mendicants from Pāvā went to the Buddha. All of them lived in the wilderness, ate only almsfood, wore rag robes, and owned just three robes; yet they all still had fetters. They bowed to the Buddha and sat down to one side.
Then it occurred to the Buddha,

segs.p: “ime kho tiṁsamattā pāveyyakā bhikkhū sabbe āraññikā sabbe piṇḍapātikā sabbe paṁsukūlikā sabbe tecīvarikā sabbe sasaṁyojanā.
segs.e: “These thirty mendicants from Pāvā live in the wilderness, eat only almsfood, wear rag robes, and own just three robes; yet they all still have fetters.

segs.p: Yannūnāhaṁ imesaṁ tathā dhammaṁ deseyyaṁ yathā nesaṁ imasmiṁyeva āsane anupādāya āsavehi cittāni vimucceyyun”ti.
segs.e: Why don’t I teach them the Dhamma in such a way that their minds are freed from defilements by not grasping while sitting in this very seat?”
Then the Buddha said to the mendicants,
“Mendicants!”
“Venerable sir,” they replied.
The Buddha said this:
“Mendicants, this transmigration has no known beginning.

segs.p: Pubbā koṭi na paññāyati avijjānīvaraṇānaṁ sattānaṁ taṇhāsaṁyojanānaṁ sandhāvataṁ saṁsarataṁ.
segs.e: No first point is found of sentient beings roaming and transmigrating, shrouded by ignorance and fettered by craving.

segs.p: Taṁ kiṁ maññatha, bhikkhave, katamaṁ nu kho bahutaraṁ, yaṁ vā vo iminā dīghena addhunā sandhāvataṁ saṁsarataṁ sīsacchinnānaṁ lohitaṁ passannaṁ paggharitaṁ, yaṁ vā catūsu mahāsamuddesu udakan”ti?
segs.e: What do you think? Which is more: the flow of blood you’ve shed when your head was chopped off while roaming and transmigrating for such a very long time, or the water in the four oceans?”

segs.p: “Yathā kho mayaṁ, bhante, bhagavatā dhammaṁ desitaṁ ājānāma, etadeva, bhante, bahutaraṁ, yaṁ no iminā dīghena addhunā sandhāvataṁ saṁsarataṁ sīsacchinnānaṁ lohitaṁ passannaṁ paggharitaṁ, na tveva catūsu mahāsamuddesu udakan”ti.
segs.e: “As we understand the Buddha’s teaching, the flow of blood we’ve shed when our head was chopped off while roaming and transmigrating is more than the water in the four oceans.”

segs.p: “Sādhu sādhu, bhikkhave, sādhu kho me tumhe, bhikkhave, evaṁ dhammaṁ desitaṁ ājānātha.
segs.e: “Good, good, mendicants! It’s good that you understand my teaching like this.

segs.p: Etadeva, bhikkhave, bahutaraṁ, yaṁ vo iminā dīghena addhunā sandhāvataṁ saṁsarataṁ sīsacchinnānaṁ lohitaṁ passannaṁ paggharitaṁ, na tveva catūsu mahāsamuddesu udakaṁ.
segs.e: The flow of blood you’ve shed when your head was chopped off while roaming and transmigrating is indeed more than the water in the four oceans.

segs.p: Dīgharattaṁ vo, bhikkhave, gunnaṁ sataṁ gobhūtānaṁ sīsacchinnānaṁ lohitaṁ passannaṁ paggharitaṁ, na tveva catūsu mahāsamuddesu udakaṁ.
segs.e: For a long time you’ve been cows, and the flow of blood you’ve shed when your head was chopped off as a cow is more than the water in the four oceans.

segs.p: Dīgharattaṁ vo, bhikkhave, mahiṁsānaṁ sataṁ mahiṁsabhūtānaṁ sīsacchinnānaṁ lohitaṁ passannaṁ paggharitaṁ …pe…
segs.e: For a long time you’ve been buffalo …

segs.p: dīgharattaṁ vo, bhikkhave, urabbhānaṁ sataṁ urabbhabhūtānaṁ …pe…
segs.e: sheep …
goats …
deer …
chickens …
pigs …

segs.p: dīgharattaṁ vo, bhikkhave, corā gāmaghātāti gahetvā sīsacchinnānaṁ lohitaṁ passannaṁ paggharitaṁ.
segs.e: For a long time you’ve been bandits, arrested for raiding villages,

segs.p: Dīgharattaṁ vo, bhikkhave, corā pāripanthikāti gahetvā sīsacchinnānaṁ lohitaṁ passannaṁ paggharitaṁ.
segs.e: highway robbery,

segs.p: Dīgharattaṁ vo, bhikkhave, corā pāradārikāti gahetvā sīsacchinnānaṁ lohitaṁ passannaṁ paggharitaṁ, na tveva catūsu mahāsamuddesu udakaṁ.
segs.e: or adultery. And the flow of blood you’ve shed when your head was chopped off as a bandit is more than the water in the four oceans.
Why is that?
This transmigration has no known beginning. …
This is quite enough for you to become disillusioned, dispassionate, and freed regarding all conditions.”
That is what the Buddha said.

segs.p: Attamanā te bhikkhū bhagavato bhāsitaṁ abhinandunti.
segs.e: Satisfied, the mendicants approved what the Buddha said.

segs.p: Imasmiñca pana veyyākaraṇasmiṁ bhaññamāne tiṁsamattānaṁ pāveyyakānaṁ bhikkhūnaṁ anupādāya āsavehi cittāni vimucciṁsūti.
segs.e: And while this discourse was being spoken, the minds of the thirty mendicants from Pāvā were freed from defilements by not grasping.
Linked Discourses 15.14
Chapter Two
Mother
At Sāvatthī.
“Mendicants, this transmigration has no known beginning. …

segs.p: na so, bhikkhave, satto sulabharūpo yo namātābhūtapubbo iminā dīghena addhunā.
segs.e: It’s not easy to find a sentient being who in all this long time has not previously been your mother.
Why is that?
This transmigration has no known beginning. …
This is quite enough for you to become disillusioned, dispassionate, and freed regarding all conditions.”
Linked Discourses 15.15

segs.p: na so, bhikkhave, satto sulabharūpo yo napitābhūtapubbo …pe…

segs.p: “na so, bhikkhave, satto sulabharūpo yo naputtabhūtapubbo …pe…
segs.e: “It’s not easy to find a sentient being who in all this long time has not previously been your son. …
This is quite enough for you to become disillusioned, dispassionate, and freed regarding all conditions.”
Linked Discourses 15.19
2. Chapter Two
Daughter
At Sāvatthī.
“Mendicants, this transmigration has no known beginning.

segs.p: Pubbā koṭi na paññāyati avijjānīvaraṇānaṁ sattānaṁ taṇhāsaṁyojanānaṁ sandhāvataṁ saṁsarataṁ.
segs.e: No first point is found of sentient beings roaming and transmigrating, shrouded by ignorance and fettered by craving.

segs.p: Na so, bhikkhave, satto sulabharūpo yo na dhītābhūtapubbo iminā dīghena addhunā.
segs.e: It’s not easy to find a sentient being who in all this long time has not previously been your daughter.
Why is that?
This transmigration has no known beginning.

segs.p: Pubbā koṭi na paññāyati avijjānīvaraṇānaṁ sattānaṁ taṇhāsaṁyojanānaṁ sandhāvataṁ saṁsarataṁ.
segs.e: No first point is found of sentient beings roaming and transmigrating, shrouded by ignorance and fettered by craving.

segs.p: Evaṁ dīgharattaṁ vo, bhikkhave, dukkhaṁ paccanubhūtaṁ tibbaṁ paccanubhūtaṁ byasanaṁ paccanubhūtaṁ, kaṭasī vaḍḍhitā.
segs.e: For such a long time you have undergone suffering, agony, and disaster, swelling the cemeteries.

segs.p: Yāvañcidaṁ, bhikkhave, alameva sabbasaṅkhāresu nibbindituṁ, alaṁ virajjituṁ, alaṁ vimuccitun”ti.
segs.e: This is quite enough for you to become disillusioned, dispassionate, and freed regarding all conditions.”
Linked Discourses 15.20
2. Chapter Two
Mount Vepulla

segs.p: Ekaṁ samayaṁ bhagavā rājagahe viharati gijjhakūṭe pabbate.
segs.e: At one time the Buddha was staying near Rājagaha, on the Vulture’s Peak Mountain.
There the Buddha addressed the mendicants,
“Mendicants!”
“Venerable sir,” they replied.
The Buddha said this:
“Mendicants, this transmigration has no known beginning.

segs.p: Pubbā koṭi na paññāyati avijjānīvaraṇānaṁ sattānaṁ taṇhāsaṁyojanānaṁ sandhāvataṁ saṁsarataṁ.
segs.e: No first point is found of sentient beings roaming and transmigrating, shrouded by ignorance and fettered by craving.

segs.p: Bhūtapubbaṁ, bhikkhave, imassa vepullassa pabbatassa ‘pācīnavaṁso’tveva samaññā udapādi.
segs.e: Once upon a time, mendicants, this Mount Vepulla was known as Pācīnavaṁsa.

segs.p: Tena kho pana, bhikkhave, samayena manussānaṁ ‘tivarā’tveva samaññā udapādi.
segs.e: And at that time people were known as Tivaras.

segs.p: Tivarānaṁ, bhikkhave, manussānaṁ cattārīsa vassasahassāni āyuppamāṇaṁ ahosi.
segs.e: The lifespan of the Tivaras was 40,000 years.

segs.p: Tivarā, bhikkhave, manussā pācīnavaṁsaṁ pabbataṁ catūhena ārohanti, catūhena orohanti.
segs.e: It took them four days to climb Mount Vepulla, and four days to descend.

segs.p: Tena kho pana, bhikkhave, samayena kakusandho bhagavā arahaṁ sammāsambuddho loke uppanno hoti.
segs.e: At that time Kakusandha, the Blessed One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha arose in the world.

segs.p: Kakusandhassa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa vidhurasañjīvaṁ nāma sāvakayugaṁ ahosi aggaṁ bhaddayugaṁ.
segs.e: Kakusandha had a fine pair of chief disciples named Vidhura and Sañjīva.

segs.p: Passatha, bhikkhave, sā cevimassa pabbatassa samaññā antarahitā, te ca manussā kālaṅkatā, so ca bhagavā parinibbuto.
segs.e: See, mendicants! This mountain’s name has vanished, those people have passed away, and that Buddha has become fully quenched.
So impermanent are conditions,
so unstable are conditions,
so unreliable are conditions.

segs.p: Yāvañcidaṁ, bhikkhave, alameva sabbasaṅkhāresu nibbindituṁ, alaṁ virajjituṁ, alaṁ vimuccituṁ.
segs.e: This is quite enough for you to become disillusioned, dispassionate, and freed regarding all conditions.

segs.p: Bhūtapubbaṁ, bhikkhave, imassa vepullassa pabbatassa ‘vaṅkako’tveva samaññā udapādi.
segs.e: Once upon a time this Mount Vepulla was known as Vaṅkaka.

segs.p: Tena kho pana, bhikkhave, samayena manussānaṁ ‘rohitassā’tveva samaññā udapādi.
segs.e: And at that time people were known as Rohitassas.

segs.p: Rohitassānaṁ, bhikkhave, manussānaṁ tiṁsavassasahassāni āyuppamāṇaṁ ahosi.
segs.e: The lifespan of the Rohitassas was 30,000 years.

segs.p: Rohitassā, bhikkhave, manussā vaṅkakaṁ pabbataṁ tīhena ārohanti, tīhena orohanti.
segs.e: It took them three days to climb Mount Vepulla, and three days to descend.

segs.p: Tena kho pana, bhikkhave, samayena koṇāgamano bhagavā arahaṁ sammāsambuddho loke uppanno hoti.
segs.e: At that time Koṇāgamana, the Blessed One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha arose in the world.

segs.p: Koṇāgamanassa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa bhiyyosuttaraṁ nāma sāvakayugaṁ ahosi aggaṁ bhaddayugaṁ.
segs.e: Koṇāgamana had a fine pair of chief disciples named Bhiyyosa and Uttara.

segs.p: Passatha, bhikkhave, sā cevimassa pabbatassa samaññā antarahitā, te ca manussā kālaṅkatā, so ca bhagavā parinibbuto.
segs.e: See, mendicants! This mountain’s name has vanished, those people have passed away, and that Buddha has become fully quenched.
So impermanent are conditions …

segs.p: Bhūtapubbaṁ, bhikkhave, imassa vepullassa pabbatassa ‘supasso’tveva samaññā udapādi.
segs.e: Once upon a time this Mount Vepulla was known as Supassa.

segs.p: Tena kho pana, bhikkhave, samayena manussānaṁ ‘suppiyā’tveva samaññā udapādi.
segs.e: And at that time people were known as Suppiyas.

segs.p: Suppiyānaṁ, bhikkhave, manussānaṁ vīsativassasahassāni āyuppamāṇaṁ ahosi.
segs.e: The lifespan of the Suppiyas was 20,000 years.

segs.p: Suppiyā, bhikkhave, manussā supassaṁ pabbataṁ dvīhena ārohanti, dvīhena orohanti.
segs.e: It took them two days to climb Mount Vepulla, and two days to descend.

segs.p: Tena kho pana, bhikkhave, samayena kassapo bhagavā arahaṁ sammāsambuddho loke uppanno hoti.
segs.e: At that time Kassapa, the Blessed One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha arose in the world.

segs.p: Kassapassa, bhikkhave, bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa tissabhāradvājaṁ nāma sāvakayugaṁ ahosi aggaṁ bhaddayugaṁ.
segs.e: Kassapa had a fine pair of chief disciples named Tissa and Bhāradvāja.

segs.p: Passatha, bhikkhave, sā cevimassa pabbatassa samaññā antarahitā, te ca manussā kālaṅkatā, so ca bhagavā parinibbuto.
segs.e: See, mendicants! This mountain’s name has vanished, those people have passed away, and that Buddha has become fully quenched.
So impermanent are conditions …

segs.p: Etarahi kho pana, bhikkhave, imassa vepullassa pabbatassa ‘vepullo’tveva samaññā udapādi.
segs.e: These days this Mount Vepulla is known as Vepulla.

segs.p: Etarahi kho pana, bhikkhave, imesaṁ manussānaṁ ‘māgadhakā’tveva samaññā udapādi.
segs.e: And these people are known as Magadhans.

segs.p: Māgadhakānaṁ, bhikkhave, manussānaṁ appakaṁ āyuppamāṇaṁ parittaṁ lahukaṁ;
segs.e: The lifespan of the Magadhans is short, brief, and fleeting.

segs.p: yo ciraṁ jīvati so vassasataṁ appaṁ vā bhiyyo.
segs.e: A long life is a hundred years or a little more.

segs.p: Māgadhakā, bhikkhave, manussā vepullaṁ pabbataṁ muhuttena ārohanti muhuttena orohanti.
segs.e: It takes the Magadhans an hour to climb Mount Vepulla, and an hour to descend.

segs.p: Etarahi kho panāhaṁ, bhikkhave, arahaṁ sammāsambuddho loke uppanno.
segs.e: And now I am the Blessed One, the perfected one, the fully awakened Buddha who has arisen in the world.

segs.p: Mayhaṁ kho pana, bhikkhave, sāriputtamoggallānaṁ nāma sāvakayugaṁ aggaṁ bhaddayugaṁ.
segs.e: I have a fine pair of chief disciples named Sāriputta and Moggallāna.

segs.p: Bhavissati, bhikkhave, so samayo yā ayañcevimassa pabbatassa samaññā antaradhāyissati, ime ca manussā kālaṁ karissanti, ahañca parinibbāyissāmi.
segs.e: There will come a time when this mountain’s name will vanish, those people will die, and I will be fully extinguished.
So impermanent are conditions,
so unstable are conditions,
so unreliable are conditions.

segs.p: Yāvañcidaṁ, bhikkhave, alameva sabbasaṅkhāresu nibbindituṁ, alaṁ virajjituṁ, alaṁ vimuccitun”ti.
segs.e: This is quite enough for you to become disillusioned, dispassionate, and freed regarding all conditions.”
That is what the Buddha said.

segs.p: Idaṁ vatvāna sugato athāparaṁ etadavoca satthā:
segs.e: Then the Holy One, the Teacher, went on to say:
“For the Tivaras it was Pācīnavaṁsa,
for the Rohitassas, Vaṅkaka,
Supassa for the Suppiyas,
and Vepulla for the Magadhans.
Oh! Conditions are impermanent,
their nature is to rise and fall;
having arisen, they cease;
their settling is such bliss.”
The Linked Discourses on the unknown beginning are complete.
